SUBJECT:  TOPICS FOR DISCUSSION DURING THE 2018 JOINT MEETING OF THE
  CITY COUNCIL AND PARKLANDS COMMITTEE

DATE:  OCTOBER 30, 2018

The following are topics for discussion during the joint meeting of the City Council and Parklands
Committee:
1. Should the fee structure for issuance of permits for tree trimming for view and /or maintenance
  be modified?
2. Can/should the City allow residents to utilize the City tree contractor in cases where they have
  been given Parklands/City approval to trim for views and /or maintenance?
3. Consideration of amending the Tree Management Policy to more specifically address tree/root
  damage to public utilities, streets, curb, gutters, walkways and driveways, when there are
  significant risks to public safety and/or welfare.
4. Designated Street Tree Policy: Waivers for different tree species and process to change the
  ‘Designated Street Tree’.
5. Oral report of City efforts to perform a street tree inventory and develop a Tree Management
  Plan?
6. Oral report of status of project to landscape the Triangle.
For the discussion of each of these items, staff has summarized and/or provided background
information for Topics 1 thru 4 above in Attachments A thru D, respectively.
Notification
The agenda for this meeting has been posted in the customary locations and in compliance with the
Municipal Code. A copy of this report has been forwarded to each Parklands Committee member.
ATTACHMENTS:
A – Permit Fees for Tree Trimming
B – Resident Use of City Tree Trimming Contractor
C – Tree Management Policy
D – Designated Street Tree Policy
E – Public Correspondence
  1
   ATTACHMENT A

  Should the Fee Structure for Issuance of Permits for Tree Trimming
  for View and /or Maintenance be Modified?

Background

On January 10, 2018, the City Council approved Resolution R18-04 adopting an updated fee
schedule for services provided by the City. The City Council determined that the City’s current
fees and charges for service should be adjusted to provide full cost recovery. In some situations,
the City Council identified a public benefit justifying a lower fee or change that provided a
partial cost recovery (e.g. block parties, appeals, etc.) The findings of the fee analysis indicated
that a $458 fee would be needed to obtain full cost recovery of services associated with a tree
trimming permit. The estimation of cost recovery was based upon a non-standard tree trim that
would require direct input and supervision by the Urban Forester and a standard trim with
minimal supervision. The Ad Hoc Committee of Mayor Pro Tem Peterson and Council Member
King specifically considered the tree trimming fees and recommended a reduced fee. The City
Council determined that full recovery placed a burden on the resident and a reduced fee of $250
could be supported since the tree trimming would also address the City’s interest in maintaining
public trees.

In summary, the City Council established the following fees:

Tree Trimming (Issuance Fee)  $250 per application
Tree Topping / Removal Permit  $458 per application
Parkway Tree Planting  $250 per application

The updated tree trimming fees become effective on March 12, 2018.

The City provides routine trimming of public trees located along the public rights-of-way based
upon need and a trimming cycle. In some cases, residents request authorization to provide a
standard trim to augment the services provided by the City. A standard trim allows for the
removing of damaged, dead or structurally weak limbs, which will improve a tree’s health and
appearance. A standard trim is not performed to enhance view and does not allow for the
aggressive removal of limbs. Residents seeking to perform a standard trim are not required to
submit an application to the Parklands Committee. An average of 15-20 no fee permits are
issued monthly to qualified contractors (D-49 license) on behalf of residents. There are likely
less requests for residents to perform standard tree trimming due to the requirement to pay a
$250 fee for a tree trimming permit.

Pursuant to the Tree Management Policy, residents are able to submit applications to the
Parklands Committee to request authorization to trim public street trees in order to improve
views. The normal practice has been for the Parklands Committee to recommend approval of
non-standard tree trimming to the City Council based upon the applicant selecting a qualified
contractor who will perform the work under the supervision of the Urban Forester.

  1
 Previously, the authorization for non-standard trimming allowed for the applicant to obtain an
annual no fee permit. An average of 1-2 no fee permits are issued monthly for non-standard
trimming subject to a prior Parklands Committee and City Council authorization. In February
2018, the City Council considered if the tree trimming fee would apply to prior actions and
should be considered for future applications submitted to the Parklands Committee. The City
Council voted to maintain no fee permits for pre-existing applications, but all future applications
were to be subject to the fee.

Discussion

Maintenance trimming is the ideal situation where the trees need little trimming to keep trees
attractive and in balance with the home and garden. Many passionate homeowners and large
managed estates prefer to maintain the landscape design and appearance by trimming the trees
annually on their property as well as in the adjacent public right-of-way. Untrimmed public trees
next to maintained properties, whether that be the street parkway or adjacent Parklands, may be
an unacceptable situation for some residents. Additionally, some home owners decide to not
trim their own trees until the City can trim the public trees adjacent to their home to keep
consistency.

With the newly adopted fee schedule, fees are now charged for the issuance of permits for
maintenance trimming performed by private property owners. Trimming public trees for
maintenance doesn’t require Parklands Committee approval. However, standard tree trimming
permits are now issued upon application and payment of the $250 fee. The Urban Forester
reviews the permit application and inspects the subject tree requested before the permit is issued;
and inspects the work to confirm standards were followed after the trimming. Many tree
trimming companies call before requesting a permit to discuss options and to confirm what is
approvable by the Urban Forester and what requires Parklands Committee/City Council
approval. This is necessary to prepare a contract proposal for their customers.

Since the effective date of the new fees, twelve tree trimming permits have been issued totaling
$3,000. Previously, these permits would have been “no-fee”. Ten of these twelve permits were
for standard trimming; two were for previously approved Parklands Committee applications that
did not specify approval of an annual “no-fee” permit.

Several residents have questioned and complained about the $250 maintenance trimming fee for
work that they feel is a benefit to the City. However, charging such fees is consistent with other
permits issued, such as the replacement of curb or driveways or other work performed by private
parties in the public right-of-way.

  2
   ATTACHMENT B

  Can/Should the City Allow Residents to Utilize the City Tree
  Contractor in Cases Where They Have Been Given Parklands/City
  Approval to Trim for Views and /or Maintenance?

Recently, there have been several inquiries from residents, asking if they can utilize Travers Tree
Service to trim tree under permit issuance for views and /or maintenance. The thought being,
that they may realize cost savings if piggy backing onto the City’s contract and unit costs.
Residents and contractors are

Discussion

The contract with Travers Tree Service for tree maintenance services doesn’t restrict who
Travers Tree Service, Inc. can enter into a contract with. Nor does it establish a pricing schedule
for Travers Tree Service to follow for private customers.

The City cannot compel Travers to provide service to private parties at current contract unit
prices in accordance with their existing contract with the City. The only way to guarantee that
tree trimming or removal approved by the Parklands Committee be performed by Travers Tree
Service for applicants at City unit prices, the City would need to issue the work request directly
to Travers and direct the work. However, this would impact existing contract limits, require
costs to be reimbursed by the applicants, and potentially increase City liability.

  1
   ATTACHMENT C

  Consideration of Amending the Tree Management Policy to More
  Specifically Address Tree/Root Damage to Public Utilities, Streets,
  Curb, Gutters, Walkways and Driveways, When There Are
  Significant Risks to Public Safety and/or Welfare

A number of cases to address tree/root damage various infrastructure have come before the
Parklands Committee. In most instances, the Committee has construed the “public safety”
language in the Tree Management Policy (TMP) to permit tree removal. The current issue is,
should there be more definitive language in the TMP?

Should significant damage to infrastructure in the public right-of-way (driveway, walkways,
curbs, gutters, streets) and the associated repair costs be considered, even if the risks to public
safety are not significant? In other words, should there be consideration of public interest and
welfare?

Discussion

The TMP provides guidance to the Parklands Committee to include public safety for each
property owner as one consideration when considering applications as stated in the ‘Tree
Management Policy’. In the Consideration section of the policy, it states, “the Parklands
Committee shall consider to the extent reasonably practicable the preservation or enhancement of
public safety”. However, there is no guidance with respect to public interest and welfare caused
by significant damage, the propensity for re-occurrence of damage, or the monetary limit
considered excessive for the associated costs to repair.

The standard used by the Committee to date has been, can the tree be root pruned and still be
safe? If the answer is yes, this means the tree doesn’t need to be removed. If the answer is no,
root pruning will render the tree unsafe or hazardous, the tree is approved for removal or the
project is modified.

Damage to public infrastructure and the costs to repair are included in the scope of work in most
cases when applications for removal are presented to the Parklands Committee. However, if
potential future damage to public infrastructure is fully considered, more trees would be
removed.

It is important to identify what is public responsibility and what is private responsibility with
respect to infrastructure within the public right-of-way. The practice has been to consider curb,
gutter and the asphalt street as public responsibility and routinely maintained by the City.
Mailboxes, driveway approaches, driveways and walkways are considered private standard
encroachments in the public right-of-way (parkway), which the City generally requires the
property owner to maintain.

Many trees throughout the City have been planted too close to the street or driveways and crack
and lift the pavement or concrete.

  1
 Common practice has been to repair public infrastructure when it becomes unsafe. Every effort
is made to retain trees; however, in certain cases tree are removed due to extensive damage to the
root system when making the repairs, such as when a roadway section is in need of removal and
reconstruction, or the replacement of curb requires significant root pruning. This decision is
made by the City Engineer in conjunction with the Urban Forester. However, in cases where
“private” infrastructure is in need of repair, the matter is generally placed before the Parklands
Committee. In most cases, the tree has been spared despite the need to construct a lesser
improvement (e.g. a non-standard feature, a narrower driveway or less thick pavement section).

Whether or not there will be damage is very predictable with certain tree types and locations.
The issue is, what should the factors or policy be to provide guidance for removal of trees
affecting infrastructure? Should tree removal in these cases be considered administratively or
administered by the City or considered by the Parklands Committee? Should this be just another
factor in the discussion or should the City place a priority on preserving the infrastructure and
proactively approve removal of trees with high potential to damage infrastructure? At what point
is it the resident’s responsibility to repair the public infrastructure? What is the City’s
responsibility to protect public or private infrastructure when tree roots are becoming an issue?
Should root invasive trees be removed on request?

  2
   ATTACHMENT D

  Designated Street Tree Policy

Discussion

Official tree, shrub and plant regulations for the City are adopted and established by Palos
Verdes Estates Municipal Code (PVEMC), Chapter 12.16.010.

12.16.010 lists twelve purposes of street trees:

  1.  Improve general aesthetic values;
  2.  Reduce traffic noise;
  3.  Deflect glare and heat;
  4.  Lower wind velocity;
  5.  Purify air;
  6.  Provide cooling shade and beauty;
  7.  Provide for the proper selection of trees to minimize trouble in sewers, water mains and
  storm drains and to prevent displacement of streets, curbs, gutters and sidewalks;
  8. Minimize interference with street and traffic lighting;
  9. Minimize the spread of disease to healthy trees;
  10. Minimize danger of falling trees and limbs onto the street, sidewalks, private property
  and people;
  11. Minimize accumulation of leaves and debris which cause unnecessary labor in cleaning
  the sidewalks, streets and storm drains;
  12. Select trees of longevity and those suitable to the environment.

PVEMC Chapter 12.16.050 governs the planting and species or varieties of street trees.
Paragraph A specifically states that parklands committee shall prepare a list of street trees which
may be planted in each of the parkway areas of the city.

The Parklands Committee has been responsible to prepare a list of street trees which may be
planted in each of the parkway areas of the City. This list shall be available to the public to aid
in the choice of trees to be planted. This list may be modified as experience indicates the
desirability of such modification.

Researching street tree lists changes indicates the Parklands Committee was actively designating
official street trees since the 1990s.The lists have been modified a number of times to remove tall
growing trees that block views, trees that develop disease and look unsightly, trees that are short
lived, tree that are not adapted to the area, trees that require large amounts of water, trees that
have a high potential for root damage to infrastructure and trees that develop large fruiting
structures.

Background

On April 7, 1993, the Parklands Committee determined to systematically evaluate the current
Designated Street Tree List. The Committee’s expressed objective in reviewing the list was to

  1
 enhance uniformity and continuity of the City’s street trees. The criteria used for designating a
street tree was defined as the following:

  •  When the designated street tree is suitable and performing well, no change is proposed.
  •  When the designated street tree does not actually exist on a street, a new tree is
  recommended, taking into account what actually exists.
  •  When there is no street tree designated, but a predominant tree exists in the street right-
  of-way, the Committee may recommend the predominant tree.
  •  When the existing trees belong to the same family but are of different species, the
  Committee maintains consistency by specifying the existing species.
  •  When the designated street tree is not predominant and mixed varieties exist, the
  Committee may recommend a new tree.
  •  When an existing street tree is non-performing or unsuitable, the Committee designates a
  street tree which can integrate with the existing trees.
  •  When there is a street for which no tree is designated, the Committee may recommend
  that no tree should be designated.

This evaluation produced the 1995 Designated Street Tree List. The new list established the
designated street tree for a majority of the streets with 40 streets undesignated or “none
recommended at this time”. The list was scheduled for review in the year 2000 as part of an
overall Designated Street Tree Policy.

The 1995 list contained 39 tree types that were required to be reviewed before a new list could be
considered. Height of the trees included on the 1995 list were one at 20 feet, three at 25 feet,
seven at 30 feet, two at 35 feet, five at 40 feet, four at 50 feet, five at 60 feet, two at 70 feet, three
at 80 feet, five at 100 feet, one at 120 feet and one at 150 feet tall. At that time, neighborhood
character seem to be the first priority and views did not appear to be a consideration. As an
example, Carob trees (40 X 40) were designated for Paseo Del Mar in the Malaga Cove area
where we presently have approved a small palm tree or a waiver of planting all together.
Chinese Elm trees (60 x 60) replaced the American Elm trees (100 x 100) on Via Almar and Via
Media. Both replacement trees are very aggressive, large, dense trees that will block view in this
neighborhood.

The list was re-evaluated in 2000 with the direction from the City Council to respect the average
roof ridge height of a two-story home in view areas. Views are wide spread in Palos Verdes
Estates and not just Malaga Cove or Lunada Bay. This meant most streets were to be changed in
areas with defined views. In view areas, trees up to 25 feet are probably the limit or slender
palms. These can be managed for view purposes with some tree trimming. Trees that exceed 25
feet could be used only in non-view areas. The criteria to designate street trees was also re-
evaluated to include all previous criteria and the following:

  1.  The maximum height of the tree must respect views and view corridors.
  2.  The street tree should not require frequent trimming for budget considerations.
  3.  The tree should not have weak wood, spines, fruit or excess pollen production.
  4.  Trees roots should have a low potential for infrastructure damage.
  5.  Proper scale for the street, home and parkway.
  6.  Unsuitable locations for tree identified.

  2
   7. Drought tolerant.
  8. Adapted to the area.

These 15 criteria are considered by the Designated Street Tree List whenever possible. Some
compromises in tree characteristics were allowed to preserve the neighborhood character. An
example of this is the Camphor trees on Via Nivel. These trees are root invasive at the highest
level but are retained as the Designated Street Tree due to neighborhood character. Additionally,
responsibly reducing a tree from 30 feet to 25 feet to maintain views and keep tree species that
are desirable may be possible.

In 2015, non-performing trees were reviewed. Some trees were eliminated and re-designated
and some streets received an optional type of tree as the designated street tree. A number of
streets have been changed in response to community input, resident petitions, tree availability
limitations, arboricultural observations and applications from residents.

The current designated street tree listed can be found here.

The option available today is to submit an application for ‘Designation of Authorized Street
Tree’ or ‘Waiver of Planting of the Designated Street Tree” to the Parklands Committee for
consideration. This can be for one address, a portion of the street and neighborhood or one
specific view corridor. The application fee is $430.
